newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia to raise EU subsidies with Fischler.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia to raise EU subsidies with Fischler.

text.p: The Australian government will this week raise the issue of European Union agricultural subsidies with EU Agriculture Commissioner Franz Fischler, Australian Primary Industries Minister John Anderson said on Tuesday
Anderson was responding to reporters' questions after opening the Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics (ABARE) Outlook conference.
"I am sure that the issue of agricultural subsidies will be the subject of discussion, as will the EU veterinary agreement and other things," Anderson said.
Fischler will be paying an official visit to Australia from February 5 to February 9 in connection with the ABARE conference.
He will meet Australian Prime Minister John Howard, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade Tim Fischer and Anderson in Canberra on February 6.
Anderson's comments on Tuesday showed hard bargaining over access trade-offs for agricultural commodities between Australia and the EU would form the backdrop to this week's talks.
Talks with Fischler in early December had stalled altogether, Anderson said.

Australia had faced real pressure from the EU to agree to a veterinary agreement based on regional equivalency in Europe which would require Australia to take products from one part of Europe if equivalent products were taken from another part.
Australia had not been prepared to accept that, he said.
Another stumbling block was EU questions about Australian commitment to trade liberalisation in relation to products such as cooked chicken meat and cooked pork, he said.
"We were facing a situation where almost in retaliation we were going to be subject to 100 percent physical checks of animal derived product at European borders," he said.
"That was a very unfortunate prospect for the dairy industry," he said, with New Zealand likely to be able to gain access in the normal way.
But new international quarantine rules also gave Australia a "very big stick to belt those who want to keep our product out of their market on spurious grounds," he said.
The rules provided Australia with a new avenue to pursue its own market access objectives through the removal of unjustified quarantine and technical barriers in overseas markets, he said.
He said Australia was making inroads -- in 1995/96 it secured new or improved market access for about 70 agricultural products in 36 countries.
